content.text: Spring Boot configures a lot for you, but it does so on top of Java and the JVM, and by rules you can read: auto-configuration reacts to the jars on your classpath and backs away when you define your own beans. Developers who skip Java get stuck the first time those rules pick something they didn't expect. This roadmap goes from Java basics to senior JVM skills in five stages, with a project and the books for each.

A team's new service runs perfectly on a developer's laptop. In production it starts without a single error, and a day later the orders from the morning are gone. The production environment never received the database URL, and an in-memory database driver had slipped into the main dependencies instead of the test ones. Spring Boot did exactly what
: with an embedded database on the classpath and no connection configured, it set up an in-memory database. Starting the app with
prints a conditions report that shows this in a minute, but only to someone who knows what a classpath and a bean are.
The belief: Spring Boot does everything automatically, so you can skip learning Java itself and the JVM and go straight to the framework.

It's easy to see where it comes from. Spring Initializr generates a project in seconds, starter dependencies pull in what a typical web app needs, and the official guides get you to a working REST endpoint quickly. You can write a fair amount of Spring code knowing only annotations.

But auto-configuration is not mind reading. The Spring Boot docs say it attempts to configure your application based on the jar dependencies you added, that your own beans replace parts of it, and that the

switch logs what was applied and why. Reading that report means knowing the classpath, dependency scopes, interfaces, annotations and how Spring creates objects. When something fails, the stack trace runs through your code, Spring's proxies and the JDK, and it's all Java. And at runtime the JVM is still there: threads, memory and garbage collection decide how your service behaves under load.
What a Java backend developer really does

Most of the work is building and maintaining REST APIs and services, often in codebases that live for many years. A typical week includes new endpoints and their validation, JPA entities and queries, transactions, Spring Security rules, integration tests against a real database, and maybe a consumer that reads messages from a queue. You also read stack traces, size memory for containers and upgrade Java and Spring Boot versions, which matters because Spring Boot 4.2

content.text: Some of these have aged. Head First Java's third edition covers Java up to 17, which is plenty for stage 1. Effective Java covers Java through version 9, but its publisher rightly notes that the advice applies to core features in any version. Spring in Action's sixth edition targets Spring 5.3 and Spring Boot 2.4, two majors behind Boot 4.2: read it for the concepts and take every API detail from
. Java Concurrency in Practice was written around Java 5 and 6; its rules for thread safety still hold, but it predates virtual threads, so read
for those. For the language itself, the free tutorials on

content.text: Every dependency you add can change what Spring Boot sets up for you. Keep test-only libraries in the test scope, set connection settings explicitly in every environment, and when a bean surprises you, start with
and read the conditions report before you add more configuration.

blocks.title: Learn on the LTS and upgrade on purpose

content.text: Use the current LTS release for learning and for your projects, and treat each upgrade, of Java or of Spring Boot, as a small project with its own branch, release notes and test run. Upgrades are a skill that seniors are expected to have.
Publish the library API on GitHub with a README, a

file that starts it with its database, and CI that runs the Testcontainers tests on every push. Add a short write-up of one performance problem you profiled and fixed, with the numbers before and after, and one of an upgrade you did. Those show the JVM and production skills that a list of annotations can't.
